L0@P0: Positivity-preserving entropy filtering for the ideal
L1@P0: magnetohydrodynamics equations
L2@P0: T. Dzanica,∗, F. D. Witherdena
L3@P0: aDepartment of Ocean Engineering, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843
L4@P0: A R T I C L E I N F O
L5@P0: Keywords:
L6@P0: Discontinuous spectral element
L7@P0: Ideal magnetohydrodynamics
L8@P0: Shock capturing
L9@P0: Positivity-preserving
L10@P0: Entropy filtering
L11@P0: A B S T R A C T
L12@P0: In this work, we present a positivity-preserving adaptive filtering approach for discontinuous
L13@P0: spectral element approximations of the ideal magnetohydrodynamics equations. This approach
L14@P0: combines the entropy filtering method (Dzanic and Witherden, J. Comput. Phys., 468, 2022) for
L15@P0: shock capturing in gas dynamics along with the eight-wave method for enforcing a divergencefree magnetic field. Due to the inclusion of non-conservative source terms, an operator-splitting
L16@P0: approach is introduced to ensure that the positivity and entropy constraints remain satisfied by
L17@P0: the discrete solution. Furthermore, a computationally efficient algorithm for solving the optimization process for this nonlinear filtering approach is presented. The resulting scheme can
L18@P0: robustly resolve strong discontinuities on general unstructured grids without tunable parameters
L19@P0: while recovering high-order accuracy for smooth solutions. The efficacy of the scheme is shown
L20@P0: in numerical experiments on various problems including extremely magnetized blast waves and
L21@P0: three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic instabilities.
L22@P0: 1. Introduction
L23@P0: The transport and interaction of a non-resistive conducting fluid and its electromagnetic field remain extensively
L24@P0: investigated phenomena as they are instrumental in various applications ranging from the study of astrophysical accretion disks [1] and supernova remnants [2] to magnetic confinement fusion [3] and plasma physics [4]. These strongly
L25@P0: nonlinear effects are governed by the equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), which are composed of a
L26@P0: combination of the Euler equations of gas dynamics and Maxwell’s equations of electromagnetism. From this formulation, a strong coupling between the magnetic field and the conducting fluid can be observed, where the magnetic
L27@P0: field induces a current in the fluid which, in turn, gives rise to a second, induced magnetic field. This interaction
L28@P0: can introduce multi-scale, multi-physics behavior in the system, such that magnetohydrodynamic flows can become
L29@P0: exceedingly complex.
L30@P0: As a result of this complexity, the robust and accurate numerical approximation of ideal MHD can present many
L31@P0: challenges. Since hyperbolic systems are known to produce discontinuities even with smooth initial conditions [5],
L32@P0: the numerical scheme must be able to robustly resolve these discontinuities which, in the case of MHD, come in the
L33@P0: form of hydrodynamic and magnetic shocks and contact waves. Furthermore, the approximation of the ideal MHD
L34@P0: equations also requires an intrinsic constraint on the solution in the form of a solenoidal magnetic field which may
L35@P0: not be satisfied by the scheme even if the magnetic field is initially solenoidal. Without a mechanism to enforce
L36@P0: this constraint, unphysical dynamics can arise in the solution which can lead to numerical instabilities. The standard
L37@P0: numerical schemes for approximating MHD flows are finite difference and finite volume methods, whose properties
L38@P0: and robustness are well-established in the literature [6–11]. However, they possess certain drawbacks in that they
L39@P0: are either difficult to extend to complex domains with unstructured grids or cannot recover high-order accuracy in a
L40@P0: computationally efficient manner.
L41@P0: A particular class of schemes which have more recently grown in popularity are high-order discontinuous spectral element methods (DSEM) as they possess the geometric flexibility of finite volume methods while retaining the
L42@P0: arbitrarily high-order accuracy and efficiency of spectral methods. As such, they provide a promising avenue for
L43@P0: significantly decreasing the computational cost and expanding the viability of simulating complex MHD problems.
L44@P0: However, due to the presence of discontinuities in MHD, DSEM approximations of these systems may introduce spurious oscillations in the solution in the form of Gibbs phenomena. Without proper treatment, these oscillations can

L46@P0: tdzanic@tamu.edu (T. Dzanic)

L48@P0-1: T. Dzanic et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier Page 1 of 24Positivity-preserving entropy filtering for the ideal MHD equations
L49@P1: result in unphysical predictions or the failure of the numerical scheme altogether. To extend to use of DSEM to MHD,
L50@P1: various numerical stabilization techniques have been proposed, ranging from artificial viscosity methods [12, 13] to
L51@P1: limiting-type approaches [14, 15]. While these various methods may be sufficient to stabilize the solution in many
L52@P1: cases, they may not guarantee that the solution will abide by physical constraints, may require problem-dependent tunable parameters, can be computationally inefficient for general unstructured grids, or may be excessively dissipative in
L53@P1: smooth regions of the flow.
L54@P1: There is significant interest in the design of numerical schemes that are “provably robust” in the sense that they
L55@P1: can guarantee that the solution will abide by certain physical constraints even in the presence of features such as
L56@P1: discontinuities, the quintessential examples being positivity-preserving schemes for gas dynamics which guarantee the
L57@P1: positivity of the density and internal energy/pressure. For DSEM, this property is typically achieved through some
L58@P1: form of nonlinear limiting or filtering [14, 16–18]. However, designing schemes that possess this property without
L59@P1: sacrificing the computational efficiency of DSEM for general unstructured grids and their advantageous scale-resolving
L60@P1: properties in smooth flow regions can be challenging. In the context of MHD, this becomes even more difficult due
L61@P1: to the additional complexity of the governing equations as well as the incorporation of differential constraints, namely
L62@P1: solenoidal magnetic fields. As such, there is a need for numerical stabilization techniques for DSEM approximations
L63@P1: of the ideal MHD equations that retain as many of these desirable properties as possible, namely that they:
L64@P1: 1. Guarantee that physical constraints of the solution are satisfied.
L65@P1: 2. Are compatible with numerical techniques for enforcing intrinsic constraints such as a solenoidal magnetic field.
L66@P1: 3. Do not require problem-dependent tunable parameters.
L67@P1: 4. Do not appreciably degrade the ability of the underlying DSEM to resolve smooth portions of the flow.
L68@P1: 5. Can be easily and efficiently implemented on general unstructured grids.
L69@P1: In this work, we propose a nonlinear adaptive filtering approach as a numerical stabilization technique for DSEM
L70@P1: approximations of the ideal MHD equations to address these points. The proposed technique can be considered as an
L71@P1: extension of the entropy filtering approach originally introduced by the authors for shock capturing in gas dynamics to
L72@P1: the ideal MHD system [17]. This technique relies on using the solution’s ability to preserve convex invariants of the
L73@P1: system, namely positivity of the density and pressure and a discrete local minimum entropy principle, to compute the
L74@P1: necessary filter strength to ensure a well-behaved solution in the vicinity of discontinuities. Extending this approach to
L75@P1: the ideal MHD system presents several challenges, primarily stemming from the treatment of the divergence-free constraint on the magnetic field. We utilize the eight-wave method of Powell et al. [7] which introduces non-conservative
L76@P1: source terms in the equation proportional to the divergence of the magnetic field. As these non-conservative terms
L77@P1: can conflict with the necessary assumptions of the entropy filtering approach, we present a modified set of conditions
L78@P1: and introduce an operator splitting approach to the system which allows the filtering method to retain its positivitypreserving properties for most practical applications. Furthermore, as the original approach for performing the optimization process necessary in the adaptive filtering framework as presented in Dzanic and Witherden [17] was found
L79@P1: to be quite computationally expensive, we develop a highly-efficient numerical approach which drastically reduces
L80@P1: the overall computational cost. The resulting approach can robustly resolve strong hydrodynamic and magnetic discontinuities in the flow without appreciably degrading the accuracy of the underlying DSEM for smooth flows, does
L81@P1: not require problem-dependent tunable parameters, and can be easily extended to unstructured grids with relatively
L82@P1: low computational cost. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated in a variety of numerical experiments
L83@P1: including smooth transport, extremely magnetized blast waves, and three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic instabilities computing using high-order approximations on both structured and unstructured grids.
L84@P1: The organization of this work is as follows. We present some preliminaries regarding DSEM approximations and
L85@P1: the ideal MHD equations in Section 2. The entropy filtering approach for ideal MHD is then introduced in Section 3,
L86@P1: and its numerical implementation and computational optimizations are presented in Section 4. Results for various test
L87@P1: cases are then shown in Section 5, and conclusions are drawn in Section 6.
